{loading ? : …}
``` ## When to use - A first load longer than about 300 ms, where the shape of the incoming content is known: a card, a table row, a list item, a comment. - A region that swaps content in place, so the layout does not jump when the real content arrives. - A page that renders several independent regions which resolve at different times. ## When not to use - A wait under 300 ms. The placeholder appears and disappears before it can be read, which reads as a flicker. - An action the user just triggered (a save, a submit); use the button's own busy state or a `spinner`, so the feedback lands where the user is looking. - Content whose shape you do not know. A placeholder that is the wrong shape is worse than a spinner: it promises a layout that never arrives. ## API | Prop | Type | Default | Description | | ----------- | -------- | ------- | -------------------------------------------------- | | `className` | `string` | – | Merged last — the shape (`h-4 w-2/3`) lives here. | All native `div` props are forwarded. `data-slot="skeleton"` and `data-motion` are always set. ## Motion contract Recipe: `data.transition`, a continuous opacity loop. It is implemented in CSS (`animate-pulse`) rather than in Motion, because a page can render dozens of placeholders and each Motion loop costs a frame callback; the pulse only touches `opacity`, so it can never trigger layout. | Phase | Properties | Token | Interruptible | | ------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------------ | ------------- | | pulse | `opacity 1 → 0.5 → 1` | `animate-pulse` (theme timing) | yes (CSS) | | reduced | same pulse, opacity only | `animate-pulse` | yes (CSS) | | none | no animation; full opacity | `animate-none` | – | Reduced keeps the pulse on purpose: M5 removes travel and scale, not opacity, and a static grey block is easier to mistake for content that already loaded. `none` stops it completely, which is what a screenshot test or a print stylesheet needs. ## Keyboard interactions None. A skeleton is not focusable and never receives input; focus stays on whatever the user was doing when the region started loading. ## Accessibility - The skeleton itself is decorative: its text is nothing, so it is not announced. - The **region** owns the state: `aria-busy="true"` while loading, removed when done. Add `aria-live="polite"` there only if the region resolves without any other change the user would notice. - Shape is a promise. Keep the placeholder's height close to the real content, or the swap reintroduces exactly the layout shift the skeleton was meant to avoid. - Under `data-motion="none"` the block stays visible at full opacity: the loading state is still communicated by shape and by `aria-busy`, never by motion alone. ## Responsive behavior A skeleton takes its size from utilities, so it follows whatever grid it is dropped into. Avoid a hard-coded pixel height on a full-width block; use a ratio (`aspect-video`) or a relative height so the placeholder matches the real card at every breakpoint. ## Performance - One CSS animation per element, on `opacity` only; no JS loop, no layout read. - The pulse is compositor-friendly, but the animation-system budget still applies: fewer than twenty simultaneously animating elements. For a long list, render one placeholder row per screen rather than one per future row. - No `will-change`: the browser promotes an opacity animation on its own. ## Notes for AI - Never animate a skeleton into the real content with a custom cross-fade; swap the children and let the container's height stay put. - Put the loading state on the region (`aria-busy`), not on each block. - Do not use a skeleton as a generic "loading…" indicator for an action; a `spinner` next to the control is clearer.
